content: Dr. Pablo Rubinstein, M.D., was a pioneer in the 1980s in the field of cryopreservation of umbilical cord blood and placental blood cells. He developed methods to freeze these cells for use in treating patients with diseases such as leukemia and genetic disorders, including Tay-Sachs disease and sickle cell anemia. He was instrumental in establishing an international cord blood banking system and has been a key figure in advancing the field of cord blood transplantation on a global scale. Dr. Rubinstein earned his medical degree from the Universidad de Chile in 1962. He completed a surgical residency at Hospital Clinico Jose Joaquin Aguirre in Chile and pursued a fellowship at M.I. Bassett Hospital, affiliated with Columbia University. Additionally, he completed an international fellowship at the National Institutes of Health (NIH) at Mount Sinai Hospital in New York. He also served as a professor at the Universidad de Chile for four years, contributing to medical education during that time. After the first successful sibling-donor cord blood transplant in 1988, Dr. Rubinstein received a grant from the NIH to create the world’s first cord blood program at the New York Blood Center. This program was designed to build a repository of stem cell units to provide unrelated, matched grafts for patients in need. In 1993, Dr. Joanne Kurtzberg at Duke University Medical Center performed the first two successful unrelated donor cord blood transplants, one of which resulted in the cure of acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL). By 2006, over 7,000 unrelated donor cord blood transplants had been performed worldwide, demonstrating the success and impact of this initiative. Dr. Rubinstein co-founded and serves as the director of the National Cord Blood Program at the New York Blood Center. Together with his wife and co-founder, Dr. Cladd Stevens, he has overseen the growth of a diverse inventory of umbilical cord blood units from donors of various ethnic backgrounds. This diversity has been critical in meeting the needs of patients from different populations around the world. Dr. Rubinstein’s medical expertise lies in the field of immunogenetics, which involves the study of genes that regulate immune responses, influence the acceptance or rejection of tissue and organ transplants, and determine susceptibility to certain diseases. He began his career as a researcher at the Lindsley F. Kimball Research Institute at the New York Blood Center and currently serves as the director of the Fred H. Allen Jr. Laboratory of Immunogenetics. He is also an adjunct clinical professor at Columbia University. Over the course of his career, he has authored more than 200 research papers on topics such as immunogenetics, cord blood banking, and transplantation. As a strong advocate for stem cell research, Dr. Rubinstein has testified before the U.S. Senate and Congress to emphasize the importance of increasing funding for this field. He has also written extensively on the subject, contributing articles and papers to advance public and scientific understanding of stem cell research and its potential benefits.
